title: A Scorebook and a Diamond Plan
bigQuestion: How did writing games down help towns far apart play and compare the same baseball?

story.title: A Pencil on the Page
story.kicker: A scorebook lies open beside a chalked diamond, and every out waits to be written.
paragraphs: A school bench sits behind the backstop. On it lies an open scorebook with a short yellow pencil. The page has a grid of small boxes. Each row holds a player's name. Each column holds an inning.

Out on the field, a worker walks a chalk cart down the line from home plate. The white line runs past first base toward the outfield fence. The diamond is measured to the rule book, ninety feet on every side.
A student volunteer picks up the pencil. After each batter, she writes a small mark in a box. By the end of the game, the page will hold every hit, every out and every run, inning by inning.

Tomorrow, the school will send the final score to the local newspaper. A reader in another town can compare it with her own team's games. A writer named Henry Chadwick helped make that kind of page common in the 1850s and 1860s.
story.think: What can a stranger learn from a scorebook page if they never saw the game?

lessons.title: Henry Chadwick
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick, an English-born writer in Brooklyn, made baseball records common in newspapers.
reading: Henry Chadwick was born in England in 1824. He moved to Brooklyn, New York, as a boy. In England, people kept careful written scores of *cricket*, a bat-and-ball game with wickets. Chadwick knew those score sheets well.

In the 1850s, Chadwick watched baseball games in New York and began writing about them for newspapers. He thought baseball needed records as careful as cricket's. He wrote for papers such as the New York Clipper and the Brooklyn Eagle.

Chadwick wrote and edited baseball guides for about fifty years. He also sat on rules committees. In 1938, he was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame. His plaque honors his work on the rules and records of the game.

words.d: an English bat-and-ball game with wickets, known for careful written scores
a person who writes news for newspapers or magazines

look.title: Two Score Sheets
look.text: On the left: an English cricket score sheet from the 1850s, with each batter's runs written in a row. On the right: an early baseball score with each player's runs and outs in a row. The two pages look alike.
look.prompt: What did Chadwick borrow from cricket when he wrote down baseball games?

check.q: Where was Henry Chadwick born?
check.why: Chadwick was born in England in 1824 and moved to Brooklyn as a boy.

check.q: Which game's score sheets did Chadwick know well?
check.why: Chadwick knew English cricket scoring before he wrote about baseball.

check.q: When was Chadwick elected to the Hall of Fame?
check.why: Chadwick was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1938.

lessons.title: The Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: A box score is a small table that lists what each player did in one game.
reading: A *box score* is a small table printed after a game. Each row is one player. Each column counts something, such as runs, hits or outs. It is called a box because it fits in a small box of newspaper type.

Chadwick is credited with making the box score a regular part of baseball writing by the late 1850s. Before that, newspapers described games in a few sentences. A reader could not tell what each player had done.

A box score let a reader check every player's part in the game. It also saved space in a crowded newspaper. Papers across the country copied the form, and box scores are still printed and posted online today.

words.d: a small table that shows each player's runs, hits and other numbers for one game
a line of boxes going down a table, each holding one kind of number

look.title: Reading a Box
look.text: A newspaper box score has nine rows, one for each player. Columns show AB (times at bat), R (runs), H (hits) and E (errors). The last row shows team totals. Below the box, a line shows the runs each team scored in every inning.
look.prompt: What could you learn about one player from this box without seeing the game?

check.q: What is a box score?
choices: a small table of what each player did in a game
check.why: A box score lists each player's numbers for one game.

check.q: Who is credited with making the box score common?
check.why: Chadwick made box scores a regular part of baseball writing.

check.q: How did newspapers describe games before box scores?
check.why: Earlier reports used a few sentences and did not count each player's work.

lessons.title: Letters and Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Scorekeepers use short letters and position numbers to write a game quickly.
reading: A game moves fast, so scorekeepers use short marks. The letter K stands for a *strikeout*. Chadwick is often credited with choosing K, the last letter of struck. Other letters stand for hits, walks and errors.
Scorekeepers also give each fielding place a number. The pitcher is 1 and the catcher is 2. The first, second and third basemen are 3, 4 and 5. The shortstop is 6. The outfielders are 7, 8 and 9.
With these marks, one small box can hold what happened to one batter. A person who learns the marks can read a scorebook kept by a stranger in another town. The marks work like a shared shorthand.

words.d: an out made when a batter gets three strikes; scorekeepers mark it with K
a set of short marks that stand for longer words

look.title: Infield Numbers in a Scorebook
look.cite: Official Baseball Rules, Rule 9 (the official scorer); common scorebook usage
look.prompt: Why might the shortstop be numbered 6 even though it sits between second and third base?

check.q: What does K mean in a scorebook?
check.why: K is the scorebook mark for a strikeout.

check.q: What number stands for the catcher?
check.why: The pitcher is 1 and the catcher is 2.

check.q: Why do scorekeepers use short marks?
choices: to write a fast game quickly
check.why: Short marks let a scorekeeper keep up with a fast game.

lessons.title: A Guide Anyone Could Buy
lessons.mainIdea: Printed guides, such as Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player from 1860, spread the same rules and records.
reading: In 1860, a New York publisher named Beadle printed a small book called Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player. It cost ten cents, which is a *dime*. Henry Chadwick edited it for many years.
Each year's guide printed the latest rules of the national association. It also printed records from the season before. A club in a new town could buy one guide and learn the whole game.

Later, sporting goods makers printed guides too. Albert Spalding's company printed an official guide for the National League starting in the late 1870s. Guides were one way a rule change reached every club at once.

words.d: a small printed book of rules and records for a sport
a ten-cent coin; cheap guides were sold for one dime

look.title: A Ten-Cent Book
look.text: The guide gives the rules of the game as adopted by the national association of clubs, the way to lay out the field, and the scores and records of the leading clubs.
look.cite: Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player, edited by Henry Chadwick, New York, 1860
look.prompt: Why would a club in a far-off town want this cheap book?

check.q: When was Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player first printed?
check.why: Beadle's guide first appeared in 1860.

check.q: Who edited Beadle's guide for many years?
check.why: Henry Chadwick edited the Beadle guide.

check.q: How did a guide help a new club?
choices: It gave the field plan, rules and records in one book.
check.why: One cheap guide held the rules, the field layout and records.

lessons.title: The Umpire Decides
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 1845 rules, an umpire has settled arguments during a baseball game.
reading: The 1845 Knickerbocker rules named an *umpire*. An umpire is a judge who watches the game and settles arguments. The rules said the umpire's decision could not be appealed. That means no one could overrule it.

Early umpires were often a gentleman chosen from the crowd or from another club. They sat or stood off to the side. They were not paid. As games grew bigger and more serious, leagues began to hire umpires.

The National League hired and paid its own umpires by the late 1800s. A paid umpire did not belong to either team. Today, the Official Baseball Rules set out what umpires decide and how they are chosen for each game.

words.d: a judge who watches a game and settles what happened under the rules
to ask someone with more power to change a decision

look.title: No Appeal
look.text: All disputes and differences about the game are to be decided by the umpire, and there is no appeal from the decision.
look.cite: Rules of the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club, New York, 1845
look.prompt: Why would a club want one person's call to be final?

check.q: What is an umpire?
choices: a judge who settles what happened in a game
check.why: An umpire watches the game and settles disputes.

check.q: What did the 1845 rules say about the umpire's decision?
choices: It was written the next day.
check.why: The Knickerbocker rules said there was no appeal from the umpire.

check.q: Why did leagues begin to hire paid umpires?
choices: because games grew bigger and needed a judge from neither team
check.why: A paid league umpire belonged to neither club as games grew more serious.

lessons.title: The Official Scorer
lessons.mainIdea: The official scorer keeps the record that counts and decides whether a play was a hit or an error.
reading: Many people in a ballpark keep score for fun. Only one person keeps the record that counts. That person is the *official scorer*. The scorer sits in the press box, away from the field.

The umpire decides what happened on the field, such as safe or out. The official scorer decides how to write it down. For example, the scorer decides whether a batter reached base on a hit or on a fielder's *error*.

Rule 9 of the Official Baseball Rules describes the scorer's job. The scorer's record becomes part of each player's season totals. That is how records from one city can be compared with records from another.

words.d: the one person who keeps a game's official record and rules on hits and errors
a fielder's mistake that lets a batter or runner move ahead

look.title: Umpire or Scorer?
look.text: A batter hits the ball to the shortstop, who drops it. The batter reaches first base. The umpire signals safe. Up in the press box, the official scorer writes E6 in the book, not a hit.
look.prompt: Which decision did the umpire make, and which did the official scorer make?

check.q: Where does the official scorer usually sit?
check.why: The official scorer works from the press box.

check.q: What does the official scorer decide?
choices: whether a runner is safe or out
whether a play is a hit or an error
check.why: The scorer rules on hits and errors; the umpire rules on the field.

check.q: Which rule in the Official Baseball Rules covers the official scorer?
check.why: Rule 9 of the Official Baseball Rules describes the scorer's job.

lessons.title: The Catcher's Mask
lessons.mainIdea: The catcher's mask appeared in the 1870s to protect the player closest to the batter.
reading: In early baseball, catchers stood well back from the batter. As pitchers threw harder, catchers moved closer to home plate. Foul balls and pitches could hit them in the face. Broken noses and teeth were common.

In the 1870s, Fred Thayer, the captain of the Harvard University team, is usually credited with making an early *catcher's mask*. It was a wire cage with padding. He received a patent for a mask in 1878.
At first, some fans and players teased catchers who wore masks. Within a few years, masks were normal at every level. Later rules added chest protectors, shin guards and helmets for catchers.

words.d: a wire or metal cage worn over the catcher's face for protection
a government paper that says an inventor owns an idea for a set time

look.title: An Old Wire Cage
look.text: A museum case holds an old catcher's mask from the late 1800s. It is made of thin iron wire bent into a cage. Leather pads sit where it touched the forehead and chin. A leather strap wraps around the back.
look.prompt: What problem was this object made to solve?

check.q: When did the catcher's mask appear?
check.why: Early catcher's masks date from the 1870s.

check.q: Who is usually credited with an early catcher's mask?
check.why: Fred Thayer of Harvard is usually credited and received a patent in 1878.

check.q: What is a patent?
choices: a paper saying an inventor owns an idea for a time
check.why: A patent gives an inventor ownership of an idea for a set time.

lessons.title: Gloves Arrive
lessons.mainIdea: Early fielders used bare hands; leather gloves spread in the late 1870s and 1880s.
reading: In the 1845 rules and for years after, fielders caught the ball with bare hands. Swollen and broken fingers were common. Some players thought using protection was a sign of weakness.

In the 1870s, a few players began wearing thin leather gloves. Albert Spalding, a famous pitcher and first baseman, wore a glove in 1877. Spalding also owned a sporting goods company that sold *gloves*.
By the 1890s, almost every fielder wore a glove. The rules did not change the diamond for gloves. They added limits on glove size later, printed in the rule book like any other measurement.

words.d: leather coverings worn by fielders to protect the hand
equipment made and sold for sports, such as balls, bats and gloves

look.title: Two Hands, Two Decades
look.text: Picture A, 1860s: a fielder's bare hands, with taped fingers. Picture B, 1890s: a fielder wearing a padded leather glove. Both players stand on a diamond with bases ninety feet apart.
look.prompt: What changed between the two pictures, and what stayed the same?

check.q: How did fielders catch the ball in the 1845 era?
check.why: Early fielders used bare hands.

check.q: Which famous player wore a glove in 1877 and also sold them?
check.why: Albert Spalding wore a glove in 1877 and owned a sporting goods company.

check.q: By when did almost every fielder wear a glove?
check.why: Gloves were nearly universal by the 1890s.

lessons.title: Illinois School Baseball
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois held its first state baseball tournament in 1940, and the IHSA took it over in 1941.
reading: The *IHSA*, the Illinois High School Association, was founded in 1900. It sets rules for school sports across Illinois. It decides who may play, when seasons run and how state tournaments work.

High school teams in Illinois played baseball long before a state title existed. They played nearby towns under shared rules. In 1940, Illinois held its first state baseball *tournament*, and Belleville won it. The IHSA took charge of the tournament in 1941.

A state tournament depends on shared records. Each school reports its scores. Games are played on fields lined to the same high school rules. That lets a team from a small town meet a team from a big city on equal terms.

words.d: Illinois High School Association, the group that runs school sports in Illinois, founded in 1900
a set of games in which teams play to find one champion

check.why: IHSA is the Illinois High School Association.

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900.

check.q: In what year was the first Illinois state baseball tournament held?
